---
title: "Interim Report: School-Based HPV Vaccination Campaign"
author:
  - Regional Public Health Unit
date: "2024-04-12"
output:
  word_document:
    reference_docx: templates/phu-template.docx
params:
  cutoff: "2024-03-31"
editor_options:
  markdown:
    wrap: sentence
    canonical: true
---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE)
library(dplyr)
library(knitr)
uptake <- readRDS("data/uptake_2024-03-31.rds")
overall <- mean(uptake$dose1)
```

Summary
=======

As of `r format(as.Date(params$cutoff), "%d %B %Y")`, `r scales::percent(overall, accuracy = 0.1)` of eligible pupils had received a first dose.
This is up from 61.2% at the same point last year. The increase is concentrated in the three schools that piloted the
new consent process (cf. Section 3), where uptake rose by approx. 14 percentage points.  Other schools showed little change.

Is the new consent process responsible? It is too early to say for certain, but the pattern is encouraging!

Background
----------

The campaign targets pupils in year 8 (ages 12--13) at all 42 secondary schools in the region. Vaccination is offered at school by visiting nurse teams; parents or guardians must return a signed consent form beforehand. In previous years roughly one in five forms was never returned at all, which was the single largest reason for non-vaccination -- far larger than explicit refusals (approx. 6% of pupils).@@T2@@

In autumn 2023, three schools (St. Mary's, Northfield Academy and the Riverside campus of Eastgate College) piloted an electronic consent form with SMS reminders.
The pilot was designed by Ms. A. Fernandes and Dr. R. Iqbal and is described in detail in the protocol (v1.3, dated 4 Sept. 2023).

Uptake by school group
----------------------

```{r tbl-groups}
uptake |>
  group_by(pilot = if_else(pilot, "e-consent pilot", "paper consent")) |>
  summarise(schools = n_distinct(school), pupils = n(), dose1 = mean(dose1)) |>
  mutate(dose1 = scales::percent(dose1, accuracy = 0.1)) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Group", "Schools", "Eligible pupils", "Dose 1 uptake"))
```

Note that the pilot schools were *not* chosen at random: they volunteered.  Schools that volunteer for such pilots tend to be those with engaged staff and above-average uptake to begin with, so a naive comparison of pilot vs. non-pilot schools overstates the effect.  We therefore also compare each school with its own uptake in 2023 (a simple difference-in-differences).

```{r did}
did <- uptake |>
  group_by(school, pilot) |>
  summarise(change = mean(dose1) - first(dose1_2023), .groups = "drop") |>
  group_by(pilot) |>
  summarise(mean_change = mean(change))
```

The average change was `r round(100 * did$mean_change[did$pilot], 1)` points in pilot schools and `r round(100 * did$mean_change[!did$pilot], 1)` points elsewhere.


Next steps
----------

* Extend e-consent to all schools from September 2024, subject to the IT security review.
* Collect reasons for non-return of consent forms in a short follow-up survey -- e.g. "form lost", "did not understand", "decided against".
* Report second-dose completion in the final report (due Oct. 2024).

---
title: "Chapter 4 -- Empirical Results"
author: "Lucía Fernández Ortega"
date: "Draft of `r format(Sys.time(), '%B %d, %Y')`"
output:
  bookdown::pdf_document2:
    toc: false
    number_sections: true
    keep_tex: true
    includes:
      in_header: preamble.tex
fontsize: 11pt
linestretch: 1.5
bibliography: [thesis.bib, packages.bib]
biblio-style: apalike
link-citations: yes
editor_options:
  markdown:
    wrap: sentence
---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE, out.width = "90%", fig.align = "center")
library(tidyverse)
library(fixest)
library(modelsummary)
panel <- read_rds("data/derived/firm_panel.rds")
```

# Empirical Results {#results}

This chapter presents the main empirical results of the thesis. Section \@ref(descriptives) describes the sample, Section \@ref(baseline) reports the baseline estimates, and Section \@ref(robustness) discusses a series of robustness checks. Throughout, standard errors are clustered at the firm level unless stated otherwise, following the recommendation of Abadie et al. (2023) for settings in which treatment is assigned at the firm level.

## Descriptive statistics {#descriptives}

The estimation sample consists of `r format(n_distinct(panel$firm_id), big.mark = ",")` manufacturing firms observed annually between 2010 and 2019, i.e. a maximum of ten observations per firm. Firms enter the sample when they first report at least 10 employees and leave it when they exit, merge or fall below 5 employees for two consecutive years. The panel is therefore unbalanced: the average firm is observed for `r round(mean(table(panel$firm_id)), 1)` years.

Table \@ref(tab:desc) summarises the main variables. The median firm has 23 employees and an annual turnover of approx. EUR 3.5 million, but the distribution is highly skewed -- the largest 1% of firms account for more than 40% of total employment in the sample. Is this a problem for the analysis? Not necessarily, but it means that unweighted averages say little about the "typical" worker's employer, and we report employment-weighted results alongside the unweighted ones where it matters.

```{r desc}
datasummary(employees + turnover_m + export_share + rd_intensity ~ Mean + SD + P25 + Median + P75,
            data = panel, title = "Descriptive statistics, firm-year observations", output = "kableExtra")
```

Several patterns stand out:

* Exporters are larger, more productive and more R&D-intensive than non-exporters, consistent with Melitz (2003) and the large empirical literature that followed.
* R&D intensity is zero for about 62% of firm-years. Among firms with positive R&D, the median intensity is 2.1% of turnover.
* The share of firms receiving the innovation subsidy rises from 3.4% in 2010 to 8.9% in 2019, with a visible jump in 2015 when the eligibility threshold was lowered from 50 to 20 employees.

## Baseline estimates {#baseline}

Our baseline specification is a two-way fixed effects model:

$$
y_{it} = \beta \, \text{Subsidy}_{it} + X_{it}'\gamma + \alpha_i + \lambda_t + \varepsilon_{it}
$$

where $y_{it}$ is log R&D expenditure of firm $i$ in year $t$, $\alpha_i$ and $\lambda_t$ are firm and year fixed effects, and $X_{it}$ contains time-varying controls (log employment, firm age, export status).

```{r baseline}
m1 <- feols(log1p(rd_exp) ~ subsidy | firm_id + year, data = panel, cluster = ~firm_id)
m2 <- feols(log1p(rd_exp) ~ subsidy + log(employees) + age + exporter | firm_id + year, data = panel, cluster = ~firm_id)
b <- coef(m2)["subsidy"]
```

The estimated coefficient in the preferred specification (column 2 of Table \@ref(tab:baseline-tab)) is `r round(b, 3)`, which implies that receiving the subsidy is associated with approx. `r round(100 * (exp(b) - 1))`% higher R&D spending. This is in line with, if somewhat smaller than, the estimates of Dr. Bronzini and Mr. Iachini for Italy (Bronzini & Iachini, 2014), who find effects of 30--40% for small firms but essentially none for large ones.@@T1@@

```{r baseline-tab}
modelsummary(list("(1)" = m1, "(2)" = m2), stars = TRUE, gof_map = c("nobs", "r.squared.within"),
             title = "Baseline estimates. Dependent variable: log(1 + R\\&D expenditure).")
```

However, two-way fixed effects estimates are hard to interpret when treatment timing is staggered and effects are heterogeneous across cohorts, as several recent papers have shown (e.g. Goodman-Bacon, 2021; Callaway & Sant'Anna, 2021; de Chaisemartin & D'Haultfœuille, 2020). Section \@ref(robustness) therefore re-estimates the effect with heterogeneity-robust estimators.

## Robustness {#robustness}

We consider four alternative specifications:

1. the Callaway & Sant'Anna (2021) estimator with not-yet-treated firms as the control group;
2. the same, but with never-treated firms only;
3. a stacked event-study design around the 2015 threshold change, which provides quasi-random variation in eligibility for firms with 20--49 employees;
4. a placebo test that assigns treatment three years *before* the actual subsidy.

---
title: "Interim Report: School-Based HPV Vaccination Campaign"
author:
  - Regional Public Health Unit
date: "2024-04-12"
output:
  word_document:
    reference_docx: templates/phu-template.docx
params:
  cutoff: "2024-03-31"
editor_options:
  markdown:
    wrap: sentence
    canonical: true
---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE)
library(dplyr)
library(knitr)
uptake <- readRDS("data/uptake_2024-03-31.rds")
overall <- mean(uptake$dose1)
```

Summary
=======

As of `r format(as.Date(params$cutoff), "%d %B %Y")`, `r scales::percent(overall, accuracy = 0.1)` of eligible pupils had received a first dose.
This is up from 61.2% at the same point last year. The increase is concentrated in the three schools that piloted the
new consent process (cf. Section 3), where uptake rose by approx. 14 percentage points.  Other schools showed little change.

Is the new consent process responsible? It is too early to say for certain, but the pattern is encouraging!

Background
----------

The campaign targets pupils in year 8 (ages 12--13) at all 42 secondary schools in the region. Vaccination is offered at school by visiting nurse teams; parents or guardians must return a signed consent form beforehand. In previous years roughly one in five forms was never returned at all, which was the single largest reason for non-vaccination -- far larger than explicit refusals (approx. 6% of pupils).@@T2@@

In autumn 2023, three schools (St. Mary's, Northfield Academy and the Riverside campus of Eastgate College) piloted an electronic consent form with SMS reminders.
The pilot was designed by Ms. A. Fernandes and Dr. R. Iqbal and is described in detail in the protocol (v1.3, dated 4 Sept. 2023).

Uptake by school group
----------------------

```{r tbl-groups}
uptake |>
  group_by(pilot = if_else(pilot, "e-consent pilot", "paper consent")) |>
  summarise(schools = n_distinct(school), pupils = n(), dose1 = mean(dose1)) |>
  mutate(dose1 = scales::percent(dose1, accuracy = 0.1)) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Group", "Schools", "Eligible pupils", "Dose 1 uptake"))
```

Note that the pilot schools were *not* chosen at random: they volunteered.  Schools that volunteer for such pilots tend to be those with engaged staff and above-average uptake to begin with, so a naive comparison of pilot vs. non-pilot schools overstates the effect.  We therefore also compare each school with its own uptake in 2023 (a simple difference-in-differences).

```{r did}
did <- uptake |>
  group_by(school, pilot) |>
  summarise(change = mean(dose1) - first(dose1_2023), .groups = "drop") |>
  group_by(pilot) |>
  summarise(mean_change = mean(change))
```

The average change was `r round(100 * did$mean_change[did$pilot], 1)` points in pilot schools and `r round(100 * did$mean_change[!did$pilot], 1)` points elsewhere.


Next steps
----------

* Extend e-consent to all schools from September 2024, subject to the IT security review.
* Collect reasons for non-return of consent forms in a short follow-up survey -- e.g. "form lost", "did not understand", "decided against".
* Report second-dose completion in the final report (due Oct. 2024).

---
title: "Chapter 4 -- Empirical Results"
author: "Lucía Fernández Ortega"
date: "Draft of `r format(Sys.time(), '%B %d, %Y')`"
output:
  bookdown::pdf_document2:
    toc: false
    number_sections: true
    keep_tex: true
    includes:
      in_header: preamble.tex
fontsize: 11pt
linestretch: 1.5
bibliography: [thesis.bib, packages.bib]
biblio-style: apalike
link-citations: yes
editor_options:
  markdown:
    wrap: sentence
---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE, out.width = "90%", fig.align = "center")
library(tidyverse)
library(fixest)
library(modelsummary)
panel <- read_rds("data/derived/firm_panel.rds")
```

# Empirical Results {#results}

This chapter presents the main empirical results of the thesis. Section \@ref(descriptives) describes the sample, Section \@ref(baseline) reports the baseline estimates, and Section \@ref(robustness) discusses a series of robustness checks. Throughout, standard errors are clustered at the firm level unless stated otherwise, following the recommendation of Abadie et al. (2023) for settings in which treatment is assigned at the firm level.

## Descriptive statistics {#descriptives}

The estimation sample consists of `r format(n_distinct(panel$firm_id), big.mark = ",")` manufacturing firms observed annually between 2010 and 2019, i.e. a maximum of ten observations per firm. Firms enter the sample when they first report at least 10 employees and leave it when they exit, merge or fall below 5 employees for two consecutive years. The panel is therefore unbalanced: the average firm is observed for `r round(mean(table(panel$firm_id)), 1)` years.

Table \@ref(tab:desc) summarises the main variables. The median firm has 23 employees and an annual turnover of approx. EUR 3.5 million, but the distribution is highly skewed -- the largest 1% of firms account for more than 40% of total employment in the sample. Is this a problem for the analysis? Not necessarily, but it means that unweighted averages say little about the "typical" worker's employer, and we report employment-weighted results alongside the unweighted ones where it matters.

```{r desc}
datasummary(employees + turnover_m + export_share + rd_intensity ~ Mean + SD + P25 + Median + P75,
            data = panel, title = "Descriptive statistics, firm-year observations", output = "kableExtra")
```

Several patterns stand out:

* Exporters are larger, more productive and more R&D-intensive than non-exporters, consistent with Melitz (2003) and the large empirical literature that followed.
* R&D intensity is zero for about 62% of firm-years. Among firms with positive R&D, the median intensity is 2.1% of turnover.
* The share of firms receiving the innovation subsidy rises from 3.4% in 2010 to 8.9% in 2019, with a visible jump in 2015 when the eligibility threshold was lowered from 50 to 20 employees.

## Baseline estimates {#baseline}

Our baseline specification is a two-way fixed effects model:

$$
y_{it} = \beta \, \text{Subsidy}_{it} + X_{it}'\gamma + \alpha_i + \lambda_t + \varepsilon_{it}
$$

where $y_{it}$ is log R&D expenditure of firm $i$ in year $t$, $\alpha_i$ and $\lambda_t$ are firm and year fixed effects, and $X_{it}$ contains time-varying controls (log employment, firm age, export status).

```{r baseline}
m1 <- feols(log1p(rd_exp) ~ subsidy | firm_id + year, data = panel, cluster = ~firm_id)
m2 <- feols(log1p(rd_exp) ~ subsidy + log(employees) + age + exporter | firm_id + year, data = panel, cluster = ~firm_id)
b <- coef(m2)["subsidy"]
```

The estimated coefficient in the preferred specification (column 2 of Table \@ref(tab:baseline-tab)) is `r round(b, 3)`, which implies that receiving the subsidy is associated with approx. `r round(100 * (exp(b) - 1))`% higher R&D spending. This is in line with, if somewhat smaller than, the estimates of Dr. Bronzini and Mr. Iachini for Italy (Bronzini & Iachini, 2014), who find effects of 30--40% for small firms but essentially none for large ones.@@T1@@

```{r baseline-tab}
modelsummary(list("(1)" = m1, "(2)" = m2), stars = TRUE, gof_map = c("nobs", "r.squared.within"),
             title = "Baseline estimates. Dependent variable: log(1 + R\\&D expenditure).")
```

However, two-way fixed effects estimates are hard to interpret when treatment timing is staggered and effects are heterogeneous across cohorts, as several recent papers have shown (e.g. Goodman-Bacon, 2021; Callaway & Sant'Anna, 2021; de Chaisemartin & D'Haultfœuille, 2020). Section \@ref(robustness) therefore re-estimates the effect with heterogeneity-robust estimators.

## Robustness {#robustness}

We consider four alternative specifications:

1. the Callaway & Sant'Anna (2021) estimator with not-yet-treated firms as the control group;
2. the same, but with never-treated firms only;
3. a stacked event-study design around the 2015 threshold change, which provides quasi-random variation in eligibility for firms with 20--49 employees;
4. a placebo test that assigns treatment three years *before* the actual subsidy.

```{r robust, fig.cap="Event-study estimates (Callaway \\& Sant'Anna). Bars are 95% confidence intervals.", fig.height=3.5}
# results computed in analysis/04_robustness.R
es <- read_rds("data/derived/es_cs.rds")
ggplot(es, aes(event_time, estimate)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 2) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high)) +
  labs(x = "Years relative to first subsidy", y = "Effect on log R&D")
```

The event-study estimates in Fig. \@ref(fig:robust) show no evidence of pre-trends: all pre-treatment coefficients are small and statistically insignificant. The post-treatment effect builds up over two to three years, which is plausible given that R&D projects take time to scale up. The placebo test yields a coefficient of 0.012 (s.e. 0.031), i.e. essentially zero!

What do we conclude? The baseline TWFE estimate appears, if anything, to *understate* the effect slightly; the heterogeneity-robust estimators give an average effect of 0.21--0.26 log points. "Crowding out" of private R&D by public money -- the main concern raised by critics of the programme -- does not seem to occur on average, although we cannot rule it out for the largest firms.

---
title: "Stop calling setwd() in your scripts!"
author: Priya Raman
date: '2024-02-29'
slug: stop-setwd
categories: [R, workflow]
tags:
  - rstats
  - reproducibility
editor_options:
  markdown:
    wrap: sentence
---

Every few weeks somebody sends me an R script that starts with `setwd("C:/Users/someone/Documents/project")`. It works perfectly on their machine and fails immediately on mine. Sound familiar? Jenny Bryan famously threatened to "come into your office and SET YOUR COMPUTER ON FIRE 🔥" over this (her words, not mine!), and she had a point.

## What to do instead

The short version: use RStudio projects (or any editor's equivalent) and the {here} package. With a project open, the working directory is the project root, so relative paths "just work". Inside R Markdown documents, which knit with the document's folder as working directory, use `here::here("data", "raw.csv")` instead of `"../data/raw.csv"`.@@T2@@

```{r example, eval=FALSE}
library(here)
survey <- readr::read_csv(here("data", "survey_2024.csv"))
```

A few related habits that pay off:

- Restart R often (Ctrl+Shift+F10 in RStudio) and never save `.RData` on exit.
- Don't call `rm(list = ls())` at the top of scripts -- it doesn't detach packages, reset options, etc., so it gives a false sense of a clean slate.
- Put package versions under control with {renv}, e.g. `renv::init()` once per project.

In a quick poll of my team (n = 14), 9 people still had at least one `setwd()` call in an active project. After a 30-min. session on the above, that went down to 1 -- and he promised to fix it by Friday. We'll see!

---
title: "Getting started with tidyspectra"
output: rmarkdown::html_vignette
vignette: >
  %\VignetteIndexEntry{Getting started with tidyspectra}
  %\VignetteEngine{knitr::rmarkdown}
  %\VignetteEncoding{UTF-8}
editor_options:
  markdown:
    wrap: sentence
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6, fig.height = 3.5)
```

```{r setup}
library(tidyspectra)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

tidyspectra provides tools for working with spectroscopic data (NIR, Raman, FTIR, UV-Vis, etc.) in a tidy, long-format data frame. If you have ever wrestled with a matrix of 2,151 columns named `X350`, `X351`, ..., `X2500`, this package is for you! The core idea is simple: one row per sample and wavelength, i.e. a "long" table with columns `sample_id`, `wavelength` and `value`, plus any sample-level metadata you like.

## Reading data

Most instruments export either CSV files with one spectrum per column or proprietary binary formats. `read_spectra()` handles the common cases, e.g. ASD `.asd` files, Bruker OPUS files and JCAMP-DX, and returns a `spectra_tbl`:

```{r read}
path <- system.file("extdata", "wheat_nir.csv", package = "tidyspectra")
wheat <- read_spectra(path, format = "wide_csv", id_col = "sample")
wheat
```

The example dataset contains `r n_distinct(wheat$sample_id)` wheat samples measured from 1100 to 2500 nm at 2 nm resolution. Protein content was determined by the Kjeldahl method (cf. AOAC 2001.11) and ranges from `r round(min(wheat$protein), 1)` to `r round(max(wheat$protein), 1)`%.

## Plotting

`autoplot()` draws all spectra, coloured by a metadata column if you ask for one:

```{r plot-raw, fig.cap = "Raw NIR spectra of the wheat samples, coloured by protein content."}
autoplot(wheat, colour = protein) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c() +
  labs(y = "log(1/R)")
```

Notice the large vertical offsets between spectra? Those are mostly caused by differences in particle size and packing density, not chemistry. Which brings us to preprocessing.

## Preprocessing

All preprocessing functions take a `spectra_tbl` and return one, so they can be chained with the pipe. The most commonly used are:

1. `sp_snv()` -- standard normal variate, i.e. centre and scale each spectrum individually;
2. `sp_savgol()` -- Savitzky-Golay smoothing and derivatives (default: 2nd-order polynomial, window of 11 points);
3. `sp_msc()` -- multiplicative scatter correction against the mean spectrum;
4. `sp_trim()` and `sp_resample()` -- restrict or regrid the wavelength axis.

```{r preprocess}
wheat_pp <- wheat |>
  sp_trim(1150, 2450) |>
  sp_snv() |>
  sp_savgol(deriv = 1, window = 15)
```

How do you choose a preprocessing pipeline? Honestly, there's no universal answer. A reasonable default for NIR is SNV followed by a first derivative, as above; Dr. Rinnan's review (Rinnan et al., 2009) remains the best overview of the options and their trade-offs. Whatever you do, choose the pipeline using cross-validation on the *training* data only -- choosing it on the test set is a classic way to fool yourself.@@T1@@

```{r plot-pp, fig.cap = "The same spectra after SNV and first derivative."}
autoplot(wheat_pp, colour = protein) + scale_colour_viridis_c()
```

## Modelling

tidyspectra deliberately does not implement its own models. Instead, `sp_wide()` converts back to a wide matrix that works with {pls}, {glmnet}, {tidymodels} and friends:

```{r pls}
X <- sp_wide(wheat_pp)
y <- wheat_pp$protein[!duplicated(wheat_pp$sample_id)]
fit <- pls::plsr(y ~ X, ncomp = 10, validation = "CV")
rmsep <- pls::RMSEP(fit)$val[1, 1, ]
```

With 10 components the cross-validated RMSEP is `r round(min(rmsep), 2)` percentage points, which is roughly comparable to the reproducibility of the reference method itself (approx. 0.2--0.3 points). Can we do better? Probably not by much: when the model error approaches the error of the reference method, further gains are mostly illusory.

## Where next?

- `vignette("preprocessing")` compares all preprocessing methods on three datasets.
- `vignette("calibration-transfer")` shows how to move a model between instruments, e.g. from a lab FT-NIR to a handheld device.
- Bug reports and feature requests are welcome at <https://github.com/chemometrics-lab/tidyspectra/issues>!

70	## Stochastic gradient descent
71	
72	With $n$ training examples the loss is an average, $L(\theta) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i \ell_i(\theta)$, and computing the full gradient costs $O(n)$ per step.  SGD replaces it with the gradient on a random **mini-batch** $B$:
73	
74	* cheaper steps, so many more of them per second
75	* noisy steps -- which, perhaps surprisingly, often *helps* by kicking the parameters out of sharp minima
76	* requires a decaying learning rate (or momentum) to converge exactly

70	## Stochastic gradient descent
71	
72	With $n$ training examples the loss is an average, $L(\theta) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i \ell_i(\theta)$, and computing the full gradient costs $O(n)$ per step.  SGD replaces it with the gradient on a random **mini-batch** $B$:
73	
74	* cheaper steps, so many more of them per second
75	* noisy steps -- which, perhaps surprisingly, often *helps* by kicking the parameters out of sharp minima
76	* requires a decaying learning rate (or momentum) to converge exactly
